name: D. E. Shaw
summary: D. E. Shaw's own interviewing guide describes a mix of behavioural questions, situational questions about scenarios you might face at work, and case studies, with questions from mathematics and computer science for quant and software roles. The firm says interviews for trading and fundamental analyst roles don't assume prior finance knowledge, and that compelling candidates tend to uphold high standards, analyse rigorously and communicate clearly and concisely.
rounds: Application review, with a code or writing sample, case study or online test for some roles
Several virtual interviews: technical, case or situational, depending on the role
looks_for: Stating assumptions and checking your reasoning as you go
Sound fundamentals in mathematics or computer science for quant and software roles

questions.text: Tell me about a time you held your work to a higher standard than anyone required.
covers: What the expected standard was and why you went further
The extra checks or improvements you made
What it prevented or made possible

questions.text: Tell me about something you learnt purely out of curiosity, and how far you took it.
covers: What sparked the interest
How you went about learning it, with depth and specifics
What you built, wrote or understood as a result

questions.text: Describe a time you explained a complex idea to someone outside your field.
covers: Who they were and what they needed to understand
How you simplified it without making it wrong
How you knew they understood, and what they did with it

questions.text: Tell me about a time you got a better result by working closely with others than you would have alone.
covers: The task and who was involved
What each person brought, including you
How the combined result was better, specifically

questions.text: Explain expected value with an example, and how you'd use it to decide whether to take a bet.
covers: The probability-weighted average of outcomes, with a simple worked example
Taking a bet when the expected value is positive, after costs
Why risk and the size of possible losses also matter, not only the average

questions.text: Explain the difference between correlation and causation, with an example where confusing them would cost money.
covers: Two things moving together doesn't mean one causes the other
A hidden third factor, or chance in a small sample, as common causes
A trading or business example, and how you'd test for a real effect

questions.text: Explain how a hash table works and what happens to its performance as it fills up.
covers: Hashing keys to slots for near constant-time lookups
Collisions and how they're handled, by chaining or probing
Why performance drops as it fills, and resizing to keep it fast

questions.text: How would you design a system that collects market data from many sources and serves it to research teams with full history?
covers: Clarifying data volume, sources, how fresh data must be and how it will be queried
Ingesting, checking and storing raw data unchanged, then cleaned versions
Handling corrections, gaps and time zones, and making past data easy to reproduce

questions.text: A program that ran fine for months suddenly runs out of memory overnight. How would you track down the cause?
covers: What changed: code, input data size, configuration or a dependency
Measuring memory over time and taking snapshots to see what's growing
The fix, a test that would catch it, and an alert for next time

questions.text: A subscription company's revenue is growing, but its number of customers is flat. What could explain it, and what would you check?
covers: Higher prices, customers moving to bigger plans, or new add-ons
Checking revenue per customer and churn by group
Whether the growth will last, and the risk if new customers aren't coming in

questions.text: Estimate how many food delivery orders are placed in Bengaluru on a weekday evening.
covers: Starting from households or working adults, and the share who order online
How often they order and how many of those orders fall in the evening
A final figure, a sense check, and the assumption you're least sure of

questions.text: Why D. E. Shaw, and what draws you to this kind of firm?
covers: What you know about how the firm works, from its own materials or people
Why rigorous, analytical work suits you, with an example
What you hope to learn there

questions.text: Which role at the firm interests you most, and what do you want to learn in it?
covers: A specific role and what you understand it to involve
The skills you'd bring and the ones you want to build
How it fits your longer-term goals

tips: State your assumptions out loud and restate the problem before solving it; D. E. Shaw's interviewing guide suggests both.
If a question is unclear, ask; the firm's guide encourages you to confirm you've understood it.
Practise telling your story out loud, including why you made each choice in your studies or career.
For analyst roles, the firm says you don't need prior finance knowledge; show careful reasoning rather than jargon.
For software roles, revise data structures, algorithms and system basics, and talk through trade-offs as you code.
If you apply for more than one role, expect to speak with several groups; keep your reasons for each one clear.
